# 2023

::: notes
0:00. Remember the year 2023. This is what it felt like to work on a
computer: set back to the stone age.
:::

## Digital Research

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Git was hard
- Manuscripts live in DOCX
- Track changes record who did what, and disappear
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
<!-- IMAGE: a stone age person using a stone tool, or a physical book press, no caption. File: img/dsn-2026/stone-age.png. Replace this comment with `![](img/dsn-2026/stone-age.png){fig-align="center" height="380"}` -->
:::
:::

::: notes
0:10. Comparing the workflows of 2023 to today, working with data,
working with code, scientific workflows: almost everything has changed.
Change and transformation is taking place in many places. What I want
to say is that 2023 was a tough time to work with Git. We had the
terminal window, we maybe had some graphical user interfaces with
buttons. But for the average scientist who is not from IT, there was
not enough time, resources, or motivation to work with these tools. The
overhead was too large to invest the time for the potential benefit
that any IT specialist, research software engineer, or data steward
tries to convince scientists of.

[Whether a researcher knows Git or not, the manuscript sits in DOCX and
the collaboration runs on track changes, which record who did what and
then disappear on accept.]
:::

## Poll

Who has sent a document where AI was used?

Hands up for yes.

::: notes
1:10. [Ask, wait for the hands, say "keep them up".]
:::

## Poll

Who can prove which parts of the document were generated by AI, and which parts by code?

Keep them up.

::: notes
1:30. [Watch the hands. Do not explain yet; the next slide asks how.]
:::

## How?

- From memory?
- Documented?
- Automated?

::: notes
1:50. [One show of hands per option. Most hands sit on memory. Name it
in one sentence: that gap is what this talk is about.]
:::

# 2026

::: notes
2:10. Fast forward to 2026. Three years that feel like light years when
it comes to scientific workflows.
:::

## Digital Research

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Git is now a language prompt away
- Commits document the history of changes
- Issues document the history of decisions
- Your AI agent is your strongest collaborator
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
<!-- GIF: a terminal window with the bouncing Claude Code icon while an agent works, no caption. File: img/dsn-2026/claude-code-terminal.gif. Replace this comment with `![](img/dsn-2026/claude-code-terminal.gif){fig-align="center" height="380"}` -->
:::
:::

::: notes
2:20. We are in the midst of a transformation where many of us don't
really know where it's heading. We don't have the answers yet, and it's
difficult to have answers. But one thing has changed: interacting with
Git has significantly lowered the barrier for anyone who is not from an
IT background. You can now use simple language prompts to interact with
Git, just as you can with any other coding language or with writing. As
we've seen, many of you have already touched documents you've sent,
with AI. Now we have no excuse anymore not to teach everyone the
underlying principles of Git, and then reward them for using it in
day-to-day scientific practice.
:::

## Declaration of AI

![](img/dsn-2026/wcri-18-boxes.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

::: notes
3:20. With reward, I'm referring to the possibility to declare what is
human, not to declare the use of AI in scientific writing. When I look
at these 18 boxes proposed for the next standard on the declaration of
AI in scientific research, what I'm missing is turning it around. I
cannot claim that when I write a scientific paper, AI hasn't
significantly touched all of these 18 areas. Then it just becomes an
activity of checking a box. And not checking it sends a different
signal than what we're hoping for.
:::

## Declaration of human

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
- A paper in 30 minutes [@spick2026thirtyminute]
- Well documented open data makes it possible
- How do we prove our work? [@barnett2026armsrace]
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
<!-- IMAGE: screenshot of the LSE Impact post "Research integrity is locked into an arms race with agentic AI slop", or the first page of Spick et al., cropped to the title. File: img/dsn-2026/lse-arms-race.png. Replace this comment with `![](img/dsn-2026/lse-arms-race.png){fig-align="center" height="380"}` -->
:::
:::

::: notes
4:10. An AI can now produce papers based on open data within 30
minutes. That is doable and feasible, it has been trialled. What is
left for us, and how do we prove what we've done and grab this
opportunity? We can track every single change that was made to
different files within a folder. We can show what was written by us,
and we can show what was written by an AI tool, an AI harness, an
agent. The declaration itself becomes rather simple and automated,
because now all changes are documented in history, and potentially
even in issues, which can be used to plan the tasks that the AI
supports us with, and which we might have significantly commented on.
For me, this is our opportunity: to use AI agents in this way.
:::

## Git for Scientists: teaching the need to know

- Read a diff
- Review a pull request
- Know what never enters a repository

::: notes
5:10. [What remains to teach after the agent took the overhead fits a
day: read a diff, review a pull request, and know what never enters a
repository. The third one matters most, because it has never been
easier to paste personal data into a chat window.]
:::

## Agents for Scientists

Handing the need to know over to the AI

- Work safely: Git lets you revert
- Experiment freely: agentic AI opens endless possibilities
- First full-day workshop on 29 September

::: notes
6:20. This month, on 29 September, we host our first full-day Agents
for Scientists workshop, where we use Claude Code. [The need to know
is handed over to the AI: work safely, because Git lets you revert,
and experiment freely.] I'm also part of the Global Federation of
Reproducibility Networks' AI working group. [Spoken in the recording,
no slide: keep or cut.]
:::

## FAIR by doing

::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
- 12 months, 5 workshops
- Git, GitHub, FAIR data publishing, agentic AI
- One day with Greg Wilson: Organizational Change for Open Science
- Anyone is welcome, especially qualitative researchers and people from non-IT backgrounds
- Express interest here
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
![](img/dsn-2026/qr-fair-by-doing.png){fig-align="center" height="330"}
:::
:::

::: notes
6:50. [FAIR by doing is a 12 month programme with five workshops on
Git, GitHub, FAIR data publishing, and agentic AI.] After learning the
basics, participants get a full day with Greg Wilson teaching his
Organizational Change for Open Science. If you have anyone in your
groups who could be interested, or aspiring data stewards and research
software engineers who want to join this dialogue on the use of AI in
scientific research, they can express interest on this form. [Anyone
is welcome, especially qualitative researchers and people from non-IT
backgrounds.] Once we have a decision by end of November or beginning
of December, we will pick up the conversation and see how many people
we can have in the programme, which runs next year over 12 months.
:::

7:40. Lastly, I want to thank you for the opportunity to talk about

looking into how we can best help scientists to use it, for their own
